analysis_trace: Trial NCT05384132 is a randomized single-blind parallel study evaluating Livfresh Dental Gel (LDG) containing EDTA as adjunct to SRP vs standard fluoride dentifrice in Stage II-III periodontitis patients. Primary endpoint: incremental PD reduction at Day 180 for sites with PD>4mm. Secondary endpoints: GI, PI, BOP reductions. No direct results available (expected 2027). Evidence from similar EDTA dentifrice study (J Periodontol 2021, PMID 33331040) showed significant PD reduction in Stage I-II maintenance patients, supporting LDG mechanism. EDTA prevents bacterial adhesion, potentially enhancing SRP outcomes. Population differences (maintenance vs active treatment) and lack of direct Phase data limit precision. SRP alone achieves 1-2mm PD reduction; adjunctive therapies typically add 0.3-0.5mm incremental benefit. GI/PI/BOP endpoints are responsive to improved plaque control. Single-blind design may introduce detection bias. Small sample (n=76) limits power. Prediction: LDG likely shows modest incremental benefits on all endpoints vs fluoride control, with higher confidence for plaque/gingivitis indices than pocket depth.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT05384132 is a randomized single-blind parallel study evaluating Livfresh Dental Gel (LDG) containing EDTA as adjunct to SRP vs standard fluoride dentifrice in Stage II-III periodontitis patients. Primary endpoint: incremental PD reduction at Day 180 for sites with PD>4mm. Secondary endpoints: GI, PI, BOP reductions. No direct results available (expected 2027). Evidence from similar EDTA dentifrice study (J Periodontol 2021, PMID 33331040) showed significant PD reduction in Stage I-II maintenance patients, supporting LDG mechanism. EDTA prevents bacterial adhesion, potentially enhancing SRP outcomes. Population differences (maintenance vs active treatment) and lack of direct Phase data limit precision. SRP alone achieves 1-2mm PD reduction; adjunctive therapies typically add 0.3-0.5mm incremental benefit. GI/PI/BOP endpoints are responsive to improved plaque control. Single-blind design may introduce detection bias. Small sample (n=76) limits power. Prediction: LDG likely shows modest incremental benefits on all endpoints vs fluoride control, with higher confidence for plaque/gingivitis indices than pocket depth.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC8033283 PMID: 33837328 Scientists at the University of California Irvine's Beckman Laser Institute & Medical Clinic have conducted the first study to show that brushing with a novel toothpaste improves symptoms in patients with periodontitis. While several recent studies show that individuals with chronic gum disease are more likely to experience potentially life-threatening complications if they contract COVID-19, a new study shows promise in addressing the main issue. Researchers at the UCI Beckman Laser Institute & Medical Clinic recently reported results of a six-month long study, showing for the first time that a novel toothpaste demonstrated medically significant improvements in the health of the gums of patients with periodontitis, the most severe form of gum disease. 1 As a part of her focus on translational research, Dr Petra Wilder Smith initiated a double-blinded study testing a novel dental gel, LivFresh Dental Gel, against an FDA-approved anti-gingivitis toothpaste, to investigate their effects on gum health in patients with early to moderate periodontitis. The six-month long study compared how the two toothpastes affected periodontal pocket depths, gingival inflammation, and gum bleeding in patients with periodontitis who were in maintenance care. The findings revealed that subjects who brushed with LivFresh Dental Gel experienced clinically and statistically significant improvements in their symptoms versus the control group that brushed with an over-the-counter, FDA-approved anti-plaque, anti-gingivitis toothpaste. Several previous laboratory and clinical studies by Wilder-Smith's group have demonstrated that the novel formulation retards on a molecular level dental plaque formation, attachment and re-accumulation at the tooth surface by increasing its negative charge. The charged surface prevents early individual plaque islands from coalescing into larger deposits, discourages plaque from attaching to the tooth surface and supports the breakup of existing plaque deposits. Thus, by inhibiting dental plaque, the novel formulation reduces the presence of the harmful plaque bacteria and bacterial products that are implicated in chronic gum disease. In individuals who brushed with the test gel, pocket depths in the gums improved in more than 80% of diseased sites. Additionally, subjects who brushed with the new formulation had 2.5 times less gum inflammation and 1.9 times less gum bleeding, when compared to the group using the conventional toothpaste. Dr Wilder-Smith said: 'We anticipate that this novel formulation, when used in combination with professional periodontal care, may revolutionise healing in the gums and maintenance of periodontal health'. analysis_trace: Trial NCT05384132 evaluates LivFresh Dental Gel (EDTA-based) as adjunct to scaling and root planing (SRP) vs standard fluoride dentifrice in Stage II-III periodontitis patients. Primary endpoint: incremental PD reduction at Day 180 for sites with PD >4 mm. Secondary endpoints: GI, PI, BOP reductions at 6 months.

Evidence sources: (1) UAB thesis (Choreftakis 2025) describing this exact trial with n=21, showing test group PD reduction -1.73 mm vs control -1.09 mm (p=0.02) at 180 days for deeper sites. PI (p=0.04) and BOP (p=0.03) significantly improved. (2) Kaur et al. J Periodontol 2021 (maintenance patients, no SRP): 6-month PD reduction 1.18 mm vs 0.93 mm control. (3) Dental Roundup review 2026 citing 6-month trial: PD reduction 1.18 mm vs 0.93 mm (difference 0.21 mm).

Evidence-role assessment: UAB thesis = direct_numeric (same drug, same design, same endpoints, same population). Kaur 2021 = indirect_direction (maintenance patients without SRP, different population but same drug/mechanism).
Mechanism: EDTA chelates calcium, increases negative zeta potential on tooth surface, reducing plaque adhesion and accumulation. This mechanism supports incremental benefit beyond SRP alone.
Uncertainty: UAB thesis n=21 is small; larger trial (NCT05384132, n=76) may show attenuated effect. Thesis result is preliminary. No published peer-reviewed results for the full trial as of cutoff.

Primary endpoint prediction: Based on UAB thesis direct evidence showing statistically significant PD reduction in deeper sites (-1.73 mm vs -1.09 mm, p=0.02), predict incremental reduction of approximately 0.5-0.7 mm favoring LDG. Probability of meeting superiority endpoint: moderate-high given prior significant result.
Secondary endpoints: GI, PI, BOP all showed significant improvements in thesis (PI p=0.04, BOP p=0.03). Predict similar directional success but with moderate confidence due to small sample.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC8033283 PMID: 33837328 Scientists at the University of California Irvine's Beckman Laser Institute & Medical Clinic have conducted the first study to show that brushing with a novel toothpaste improves symptoms in patients with periodontitis. While several recent studies show that individuals with chronic gum disease are more likely to experience potentially life-threatening complications if they contract COVID-19, a new study shows promise in addressing the main issue. Researchers at the UCI Beckman Laser Institute & Medical Clinic recently reported results of a six-month long study, showing for the first time that a novel toothpaste demonstrated medically significant improvements in the health of the gums of patients with periodontitis, the most severe form of gum disease. 1 As a part of her focus on translational research, Dr Petra Wilder Smith initiated a double-blinded study testing a novel dental gel, LivFresh Dental Gel, against an FDA-approved anti-gingivitis toothpaste, to investigate their effects on gum health in patients with early to moderate periodontitis. The six-month long study compared how the two toothpastes affected periodontal pocket depths, gingival inflammation, and gum bleeding in patients with periodontitis who were in maintenance care. The findings revealed that subjects who brushed with LivFresh Dental Gel experienced clinically and statistically significant improvements in their symptoms versus the control group that brushed with an over-the-counter, FDA-approved anti-plaque, anti-gingivitis toothpaste. Several previous laboratory and clinical studies by Wilder-Smith's group have demonstrated that the novel formulation retards on a molecular level dental plaque formation, attachment and re-accumulation at the tooth surface by increasing its negative charge. The charged surface prevents early individual plaque islands from coalescing into larger deposits, discourages plaque from attaching to the tooth surface and supports the breakup of existing plaque deposits. Thus, by inhibiting dental plaque, the novel formulation reduces the presence of the harmful plaque bacteria and bacterial products that are implicated in chronic gum disease. In individuals who brushed with the test gel, pocket depths in the gums improved in more than 80% of diseased sites. Additionally, subjects who brushed with the new formulation had 2.5 times less gum inflammation and 1.9 times less gum bleeding, when compared to the group using the conventional toothpaste. Dr Wilder-Smith said: 'We anticipate that this novel formulation, when used in combination with professional periodontal care, may revolutionise healing in the gums and maintenance of periodontal health'. Larger and longer studies are now in progress to solidify these findings. Reference 1. Kaur M, Geurs N C, Cobb C M et al. {"url": "https://digitalcommons.library.uab.edu/etd-collection/7343/", "content_type": "text/html; charset=UTF-8", "text": "--> Home Search Browse Collections My Account About Digital Commons Network™ Skip to main content powered by UAB Libraries Home About FAQ My Account < Previous Next >   Home > UAB Theses & Dissertations > All ETDs from UAB > 7343 Randomized Control Trial Of A Novel Dental Gel As An Adjunct To Scaling And Root Planing In Subjects With Stage Ii & Iii Periodontitis Authors Efstratios Choreftakis , University of Alabama at Birmingham Advisor(s) Maninder Kaur Committee Member(s) Amjad Javed Maria Geisinger Nicolaas Geurs Ramzi Abou-Arraj School School of Dentistry Document Type Thesis Department (new version) Dentistry Date of Award 9-11-2025 Abstract Scaling and root planing (ScRP) is the gold standard for non-surgical periodontal therapy, yet no dentifrice has been definitively shown to improve its outcomes. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of LivFresh Dental Gel as an adjunct to ScRP in patients with Stage II and III periodontitis. Twenty-one participants were assigned to either a test group using LivFresh Dental Gel or a control group using a standard sodium fluoride dentifrice. Clinical parameters—including probing depth (PD), clinical attachment level (CAL), gingival index (GI), plaque index (PI), and bleeding on probing (BOP)—were assessed at baseline, 30, 90, and 180 days. The primary outcome was PD reduction at 180 days in sites with baseline PD ≥4 mm. Secondary outcomes included changes in GI, PI, BOP, and CAL. Both groups showed significant PD reductions from baseline; however, the test group demonstrated greater PD reduction in deeper sites (−1.73 mm vs. −1.09 mm; p = 0.02). At 180 days, the test group also showed significantly greater improvements in PI (p = 0.04) and BOP (p = 0.03), with no adverse effects reported. These findings suggest that LivFresh Dental Gel may enhance periodontal therapy outcomes when used alongside SRP. Larger and longer-term studies are warranted to confirm these results and explore the potential of this adjunct in reducing the need for surgical intervention. The short answer our research supports is that it’s neither. The gel produces an effect users feel on the first brush, it costs several times what proven alternatives cost, a meaningful minority of users report new tooth sensitivity, and the company’s marketing percentages don’t survive contact with the company’s own studies. We read every published trial, 17 Reddit threads across 7 communities, and all 51 Trustpilot reviews to sort out who this product actually fits, and which of the six versions to buy if it fits you. If you landed here comparing fluoride-free brands more broadly, our Boka review and hydroxyapatite toothpaste guide cover the other side of that shelf. How We Evaluated LivFresh The published evidence, not the marketing numbers. LivFresh’s site claims it “removes 250% more plaque” and reduces gum bleeding “400% better.” We traced both figures to their source studies, read the funding statements, and report what the papers actually measured. Real buyer experiences, both directions. We banked verbatim quotes from 17 Reddit threads, Trustpilot, and Walmart reviews, from ten-year loyalists to people whose gum measurements got worse. Where reviews looked planted (and we found two near-identical promotional comments posted a day apart from different accounts), we excluded them. Side-effect signal. Sensitivity reports recur often enough in the community record to be a pattern, not noise. We weighed how often they appear, whether they resolve after stopping, and what mechanism might explain them. Value against what it was tested against. The brand’s own strongest study compared it to toothpastes that cost about $2 per ounce. We priced LivFresh per ounce, per month, and per year against those same comparators. Fit, not verdict. A product with this many delighted long-term users and this many burned buyers isn’t simply good or bad. We tried to work out which camp you’re likely to land in before you spend the money. Community research · 1,486 threads LivFresh's reviews are unusually polarized. Counting all 51 Trustpilot reviews ourselves, 23 were 5-star and 21 were 1-star, with only 7 in between; one reviewer put it best: 'lots of 5s, lots of 1s, with almost nothing in between.' The pattern has an explanation. Most 5-star reviews are about the gel, and most 1-star reviews are about ordering from the brand's own website (billing, subscriptions, shipping). In the gum-health threads behind our research , the product and the company earn different grades, which is why where you buy it matters as much as whether you buy it. Does the Science Hold Up? LivFresh’s active idea is a chelating agent called activated edathamil, which is a form of EDTA, a common food and cosmetic preservative. Instead of scrubbing plaque off with abrasives, the gel is designed to weaken the bond between plaque and the tooth surface so brushing removes more of it and new plaque attaches more slowly. That mechanism is why the gel contains no abrasives at all, and it’s the source of the “squeaky clean” feel that shows up in nearly every user report, positive and negative alike. The two studies worth taking seriously Strip away the trade-press write-ups and small pilot studies, and two randomized controlled trials carry the evidence base. Both were published in the Journal of Periodontology , and both deserve an asterisk you should know about before the numbers. The first, a 2021 six-month trial in 65 people with early periodontitis , found the fluoride-free gel reduced gum pocket depths by 1.18 mm versus 0.93 mm for a stannous fluoride comparison paste. Both groups improved substantially; the difference between them was 0.21 mm, which is statistically significant but roughly the width of two sheets of paper, on a measurement dentists typically record to the nearest millimeter. The gel also showed significant improvements on gum inflammation and bleeding measures. The result stands statistically; it is also smaller than the marketing suggests. The second is the study behind the “400% better” claim: a 2023 five-arm trial in 150 people that tested the stannous fluoride version of the gel (now sold as Gum Protect+) against four toothpastes over three months. The LivFresh arm reduced gum bleeding by 47.4% from baseline, and it beat every comparator with strong statistical significance. Here’s the arithmetic the marketing leaves out: the 400% figure comes from comparing against the weakest arm in the study, a budget sodium fluoride gel that improved bleeding by 8.3%. Against Crest Pro-Health, the strongest comparator in the same table, the margin was about 1.7 times, not 5.7. Both are wins. Only one of them is the number on the box. The asterisk on both trials: the 2023 study’s funding statement names Livionex, the company that makes LivFresh, among its funders (the paper’s own conflict-of-interest line states the authors report none), and its first author now appears as a featured endorser on the product’s sales page. The studies were run at credible universities and published in the field’s flagship journal, so this is disclosure, not disqualification. But no independent research group has replicated these results, and you should weigh a manufacturer-funded evidence base accordingly. What the evidence doesn’t show (The “250%” claim, for its part, traces to small early studies in a low-authority journal; the published figure in the cited crossover study is 45% less plaque, measured against a triclosan toothpaste that no longer exists on the US market.) Three things the record is clear about. First, the brand’s own enamel studies found no remineralization advantage over ordinary fluoride toothpaste, and the sales page’s claim that it remineralizes better than nano-hydroxyapatite has no published study behind it that we could locate. Second, the fluoride-free gels have no published evidence of cavity prevention; a completed 2020 clinical trial in children that measured cavity outcomes has never reported results, so the question stays open. Third, no LivFresh product holds the ADA Seal of Acceptance . We checked the ADA’s current Seal directory directly: the market-leading comparison pastes in the brand’s own 2023 study, including Crest Pro-Health and Colgate Total, hold the Seal, and no LivFresh product does. A former ADA president does personally endorse LivFresh, and that’s true as stated, but a personal endorsement is not an ADA endorsement, and the two are easy to blur at ad speed. Professional opinion in our research also ran unfavourable on balance: a dental-hygiene instructor whose students studied the product reported negative takeaways, a board-certified periodontist objected to the advertising while relaying that colleagues found the clinical claims sound, and the dentistry-forum verdicts from 2020 were blunter still. Real counter-voices exist, including a hygienist who recommends it daily and users whose own hygienists confirmed improvement, but if you polled the professionals in our research, the product would lose the vote. On the “is it FDA approved?” question the precise answer is: no toothpaste is FDA approved. The fluoride-free gels are cosmetics. Gum Protect+ is a registered over-the-counter drug under the FDA’s toothpaste monograph, because stannous fluoride is a recognized anticavity and antigingivitis active, which is a routine regulatory status, not an approval, and not unique to LivFresh. The “400%” source: a 2023 five-arm randomized trial , part-funded by the manufacturer, in which the stannous fluoride LivFresh formula cut gum bleeding 47.4% from baseline versus 8.3% for the weakest comparator and 28.0% for the strongest.
